Packages that do not declare `lockscreen.net` (including 2.0–2.22 packages) keep their lock-screen behaviour unchanged. Only packages with `api` 2.23 or later may declare it.

**2.24** (proposal 0031) relaxes the limit: the maximum length of a single request header value in `ctx.net:request` rises from 1024 bytes to 8192 bytes, and all names and values together are ≤ 17408 bytes (section 14). No new calls, fields or error codes are added. On a host that implements 2.24, `ctx.api.minor` is 24, and the same applies to 2.0–2.23 packages; on older hosts, a value over 1024 bytes still returns `invalid_argument`. The WebSocket request header rules do not change.

**2.25** (proposal 0032) adds: desktop widgets (section 33). The manifest `widgets` declares widgets; `ctx.widget:publish / clear / options / sizes` pushes a snapshot, and the desktop and lock screen interpret and display it by the current time without running the app's script; when a widget is tapped to open the app, `ctx.launch` gives the source. Only packages with `api` 2.25 or later may declare `widgets`; `ctx.widget` exists only on devices with a dynamic desktop.

**2.26** (proposal 0033) relaxes the limit: a single request header value in `ctx.net:request` is no longer limited on its own, and all names and values together are ≤ 65536 bytes (section 14). No new calls, fields or error codes are added. On a host that implements 2.26, `ctx.api.minor` is 26, and the same applies to 2.0–2.25 packages; on older hosts, a value over the respective limit still returns `invalid_argument`. The WebSocket request header rules do not change.

**2.27** (proposal 0034) adds: the `ctx.system:open` targets `"cloud.sync"`, `"settings.font"`, and `"settings.keyboard_dict"` (section 25 "Cloud sync, fonts, and keyboard dictionary (2.27)"), which open the cloud sync page, the app font page, and the keyboard dictionary download page respectively; when the user returns, the app comes back (as a new session). Use `can_open` to tell whether the host supports this without looking at `ctx.api.minor`. It is required, the manifest does not change, and no new error codes, permissions or capability names are added. 2.0–2.26 packages can use it too.

**2.28** (proposal 0035) adds: the text parameters `italic`, `underline`, and `strike` (section 7 "Italic, underline and strikethrough (2.28)"); `g:text` and `g:text_box` draw fake italics (sheared to the right by about 18%), underlines, and strikethrough; the results of `measure` and `layout` do not change. It is required, the manifest does not change, and no new error codes, permissions or capability names are added. On a host that implements 2.28, `ctx.api.minor` is 28. It depends only on the manifest `api`: it takes effect when the manifest specifies 2.28 or later, and in a 2.0–2.27 package these are ignored even if written, with no change to the output.

**2.28.1** (proposal 0036, host behaviour, no minor version bump): presentations during `ctx:defer_full_refresh` now count toward the automatic full-refresh total, and when the count reaches twice the interval the host performs a full refresh during the deferral too (section 5). Calls, parameters, and return values are unchanged, and it applies to packages of all versions. Why: an app kept renewing the deferral, so a real device's screen never full-refreshed, and ghosting became severe.

**2.33.1** (host behaviour, no minor version bump): `ctx.screen:set_orientation` also accepts `"portrait_inverted"` and `"landscape_inverted"` (section 3), turned 180°, while `ctx.screen.orientation` still reports `portrait` / `landscape`. It applies to packages of all versions; older hosts return `nil, "invalid_argument"`. The Gancao firmware has done this since 11-06; the contract records it now.

**2.33.2** (host behaviour, no minor version bump): the optional capability `shake` and `ctx.device:shake()` (sections 13 and 17), which take one shake-to-turn action and return `0` / `-1` / `1`. Today only the X4 Classic firmware provides it; on other devices `ctx.capabilities.shake` is not true and `ctx.device.shake` is nil. It applies to packages of all versions; check the capability. In the same version, the four bottom keys of the X4 Classic deliver semantic keys in the factory order while an app is in the foreground, regardless of the system's bottom-key customization (section 4).

**2.29** (proposal 0038) adds: the `clock` field of a desktop widget snapshot (which the host fills in by the device's local time and format), and the layout's `digits` (digit atlas) and `hands` (hour and minute hands) nodes (section 33 "Current time", "Digit atlas", "Hands"). It is required, and no new error codes, permissions or capability names are added. On a host that implements 2.29, `ctx.api.minor` is 29. A package whose layout uses `digits` or `hands` must write `api` 2.29 or later, or installation is refused; for a 2.28-or-earlier package, a pushed `clock` field is treated as an ordinary table.

**2.30** (proposal 0037) adds: the Bluetooth gamepad (section 4 "Gamepad (2.30)"): `gamepad` in `listen`, key events with `source = "gamepad"`, `ctx.input:gamepad()` (required, and 2.10–2.29 packages can also use it), and `ctx.input:set_gamepad_adapter`, which needs the new permission `gamepad` (only packages with `api` 2.30 or later may declare it). When no adapter is bound and no gamepad is listened for, the behaviour of the system and old apps does not change. No new error codes or capability names are added; `cancelled` appears only as the `err` of a completion function. On a host that implements 2.30, `ctx.api.minor` is 30.

**2.31** (proposal 0039) adds: public folders (section 29 "Public folders (2.31)"): `ctx.files:folder(name)`, which needs the new permission `folders`, and the folder object (`path`, `list`, `exists`, `size`, `read`, `write`, `append`, `remove`, `mkdir`, `rmdir`), which reads and writes the nine fixed folders in the storage card's root directory, five of which can have subfolders. It is required; `folders` may be declared only by packages with `api` 2.31 or later, and an older host refuses to install them as an unknown permission. No new error codes or capability names are added. On a host that implements 2.31, `ctx.api.minor` is 31.

**2.32** (proposal 0040) adds: installed apps (section 34): `ctx.apps:list()`, `recent(n)`, and `icon(id)`, which need the new permission `apps`; the `ctx.system:open` target `"app"` (section 25 "Opening another app (2.32)", which also needs `apps`), which opens another app, and when it ends the app comes back, with `ctx.launch` as `{ source = "app", from, open }`; and `ctx.system:act(name)` (section 25 "System actions (2.32)") with `sleep`, `power_off` (system-confirmed), and `refresh`, the first two available only during a user action. It is required; `apps` may be declared only by packages with `api` 2.32 or later, and an older host refuses to install them as an unknown permission; `act` needs no permission, and 2.0–2.31 packages can use it too. No new error codes or capability names are added. On a host that implements 2.32, `ctx.api.minor` is 32.

**2.33** (proposal 0041) adds: the library and the cover (section 22): `ctx.reader:library(opts)` lists, page by page, every book on the storage card (the system bookshelf's index, including books that have not been opened), and only packages that declare `api` 2.33 or later have it; `ctx.reader:cover(id, opts)` with `opts.source = "epub"` takes the cover image directly from the EPUB file without looking at the cache (for a 2.0–2.32 package that writes `opts`, the host ignores it); and `ctx.system:open("book")` (section 25) also accepts a `library()` book for a 2.33 package. A host fix that applies to packages of all versions: when `g:image`'s `src` has no `x` field, it reads `{ x, y, w, h }` by position (section 6). No new permissions, error codes or capability names are added, and `reader` is used as before. The package size limit rises from 32 MB to 128 MB (appendix A). On a host that implements 2.33, `ctx.api.minor` is 33.

# 20. Conformance tests

Each section has a corresponding set of test apps. The tests run on the host's simulator and on hardware, and the log prints `api2 <section> passed checks=<n>`. Drawing results are compared pixel by pixel against the golden image for each device profile.

A host that claims to support 2.m must pass every test except those in section 17, and must pass the tests for every optional capability it reports as true. A rule with no test cannot enter a release.

| 2.33: read every book on the storage card (paging, sorting, filtering by status and format), including books never opened; take the cover straight from the EPUB without opening it in the reader or on the shelf first; any book in the library can be opened; the `src` of `g:image` can also be written by position | 6, 22, 25 |
| 2.33.2 (optional capability `shake`, today only the X4 Classic): shake the device to turn pages, with the same direction and switch as the reader | 13, 17 |
| 2.18: general FWNN v1/v2/v3 model inference and format query, F32LE outside and INT8/INT32 or I8 weights with F32 activations inside; runs in slices with cancel and deadline, and the model, scratch, and job are held to fixed limits | 30 |

# 22. Reading data (2.1)

Requires the `reader` permission and the `reader` optional capability; otherwise `ctx.reader` is nil. Both the main program and lock-screen sessions can use it. It is read-only.

```lua
local books = ctx.reader:books()            -- recently read books, most recent first
local book  = ctx.reader:current()          -- the book being read, or the most recent; nil if there is none
local days  = ctx.reader:days("2026-10-05", "2026-10-11")
local sum   = ctx.reader:summary()
local cover, err = ctx.reader:cover(book.id)
local rows  = ctx.reader:book_days("2026-10-05", "2026-10-11")   -- 2.8
local all   = ctx.reader:all_books()                              -- 2.8
local page  = ctx.reader:library({ sort = "title", limit = 30 })   -- 2.33
local epub  = ctx.reader:cover(id, { source = "epub", max_w = 160 }) -- 2.33
```

**Books.** `books()` returns an array of at most 18 books, ordered by most recent reading. If there are no books, it returns an empty table. `current()` returns the book being read right now; otherwise it returns the most recently read book, or nil if no book has ever been read. Both return the same kind of table:

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `id` | The book's id: an opaque string that is stable across sessions |
| `title` | Title |
| `author` | Author, or `""` when unknown |
| `format` | `"epub"`, `"txt"`, or `"xtc"`; more values may be added later |
| `percent` | Reading progress, an integer 0–100 |
| `page` `total_pages` | Page number and page count; nil before the book has been paginated |
| `finished` | Whether the book has been finished |
| `read_sec` | Total seconds spent reading this book |

**Time per day.** The dates of `days(from, to)` are `"YYYY-MM-DD"` strings, inclusive at both ends, spanning at most 366 days. It returns an array with one item per day, `{ date, sec }`. Days with no reading are included, with `sec` 0. You can compute week, month, and year totals and bar charts from this array. A malformed date, a date that does not exist (such as 30 February), `from` later than `to`, or a range of more than 366 days returns `nil, "invalid_argument"`.

**Totals.** `summary()` returns:

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `total_sec` | Total reading seconds |
| `today_sec` | Seconds read today; nil when the clock is not valid |
| `days_read` | Number of days on which something was read |
| `streak_days` `best_streak_days` | The current run of reading days, and the longest run |
| `books_finished` | Number of books finished |
| `books_read` | (2.8) Number of books read: books with a reading record in the reading statistics, including deleted ones |
| `first_date` | The date of the first reading record; nil when there is none |

**Cover.** `cover(id)` synchronously returns the cover already generated for this book (a runtime image, section 8) without opening the book file. The host chooses the size; scale it with the `w` and `h` of `g:image` when drawing. If `id` is unknown, or the book does not have a generated cover yet (it has never been shown on the shelf), it returns `nil, "not_found"`.

(2.33) `cover(id, opts)` takes one extra optional table. When `opts.source` is `"cache"` (the default), it is the same as `cover(id)`. When it is `"epub"`, it does not look at the cache; it opens the book's EPUB file right now, takes the image marked as the cover inside the book, and decodes it into a runtime image using the rules of `ctx.image:decode` (section 27): `opts.max_w` and `opts.max_h` scale it down proportionally (defaulting to the screen size), and `opts.gray` is the same as there. A cover image inside a book can be up to 2048 on a side. `id` can be any book given by `books()`, `current()`, or `library()`, including a book that has never been opened. Reading the file takes time; when a screen needs many covers, fetch them over several frames and keep the images yourself. The result is not written to the system's cover cache, so a later `cover(id)` will not hit it because of this.

| Case | Return |
| --- | --- |
| `source` is neither `"cache"` nor `"epub"`; `max_w` or `max_h` is not a positive integer; `gray` is not a boolean | `nil, "invalid_argument"` |
| `id` is unknown, or the book file has been deleted; the EPUB has no cover image | `nil, "not_found"` |
| This book is not an EPUB | `nil, "not_supported"` |
| The cover image format is unsupported, corrupt, or too large | `nil, "invalid_argument"` |
| The runtime images are full (section 8) | `nil, "limit_exceeded"` |

A package written for 2.0–2.32 that passes `opts` has it ignored by the host; the behavior is the same as `cover(id)`.

**Library (2.33).** `library(opts)` lists all the books on the storage card, the same as the system shelf's "All", including books that have never been opened. Only packages that declare `api` of at least 2.33 have this method; on older packages `ctx.reader.library` is nil. `opts` can be omitted, and all of its fields are optional:

| Field | Value | Default |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `offset` | The index of the first book, an integer ≥ 0 | 0 |
| `limit` | At most this many books, an integer 1–50 | 20 |
| `sort` | `"recent"` most recently read first, with unread ones after, by title; `"added"` most recently placed on the card first; `"title"`; `"author"`; `"size"` largest first | `"recent"` |
| `status` | `"all"` `"unread"` `"reading"` `"finished"` | `"all"` |
| `format` | `"all"` `"epub"` `"txt"` `"xtc"` (including `xtch` and `xtcz`) | `"all"` |

It returns `{ total, books }`: `total` is the number of books matching `status` and `format`, and does not change with paging; `books` is at most `limit` books starting from `offset`, and is an empty table when `offset` is not less than `total`. Each book:

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `id` | The book's id; a recently read book has the same `id` as in `books()`. It can be used with `cover(id, opts)` and `ctx.system:open("book", { id })` (section 25) |
| `title` `author` | Title and author; author is `""` when unknown |
| `format` | `"epub"` `"txt"` `"xtc"` |
| `status` | `"unread"` `"reading"` `"finished"` |
| `percent` | Reading progress, an integer 0–100 |
| `size` | File size in bytes |
| `added` | When this book appeared on the card (Unix seconds); nil when unknown |
| `file` | The file name, without folders |
| `has_cover` | true when the book is an EPUB and the system shelf has not marked it as "no cover available"; being true does not guarantee one can be retrieved |

The data comes from the system shelf's index, and it does not scan the storage card when called; a book the user has just copied in only appears after the index is updated. During the first index build after inserting a card (the system shelf shows "Organizing"), it returns `nil, "busy"`; try again a bit later. With no storage card it returns `nil, "not_found"`. Invalid field values return `nil, "invalid_argument"`; `opts` that is neither a table nor nil raises a Lua error (section 0). Out of memory returns `nil, "out_of_memory"`.

`library()` is read-only. It does not make the system generate covers, and it does not change the shelf's ordering or filtering.

**Time per book per day (2.8).** The dates of `book_days(from, to)` follow the same rules as `days`. It returns an array of `{ date, id, title, sec }` items, each meaning that on `date` the book was read for `sec` seconds (greater than 0). Days without reading have no items. Items are ordered by date, earliest first; within a day, the book read longest comes first. `id` matches that book's `id` in `books()`, and `title` is the title recorded in the reading statistics. A malformed date returns `nil, "invalid_argument"`. Out of memory returns `nil, "out_of_memory"`.

**Every book read (2.8).** `all_books()` returns every book that has a reading record in the reading statistics, most recently read first, without the limit of 18 (the statistics keep at most 512 books). Each item:

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `id` `title` | Same as in `book_days` |
| `sec` | Total reading seconds |
| `first_date` `last_date` | The first and last dates the book was read, `"YYYY-MM-DD"` |
| `finished` | Whether the book has been finished |

It reads only the statistics and does not scan the storage card, so it remains fast even with many books. Books whose files have been deleted are still listed. If there are no records, it returns an empty table. Out of memory returns `nil, "out_of_memory"`. The number of books equals `summary().books_read`.

A failed read returns `nil, "io_error"`.

**Opening a book (2.20).** `ctx.system:open("book", { id = book.id })` (section 25) opens the book given by `books()` or `current()` in the reader, and returns to this app when reading finishes. From 2.33 on, it can also open any book given by `library()`.

# 23. System dialogs (2.1)

Optional capability `dialog`.

```lua
ctx.dialog:confirm({ title = "Delete the record", message = "This cannot be undone.", ok_text = "Delete" },
  function(ctx, ok) if ok then remove_record() end end)

ctx.dialog:choose({ title = "Sort", items = { "By time", "By name" }, selected = 1 },
  function(ctx, index) if index then sort_by = index; ctx:invalidate() end end)

ctx.dialog:toast("Saved")
```

`confirm` and `choose` behave like text input in section 4: after the current callback returns, the host opens the dialog and the app receives `on_pause`; after the user makes a choice, the app receives `on_resume`, and then the completion function is called once as a callback. While the dialog is open, the app receives no input events. Back acts as cancel.

| Call | Fields | Second argument of the completion function |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `confirm` | `title` (≤ 95 bytes), `message` (≤ 191), `ok_text`, `cancel_text` (each ≤ 63; defaults to the system's Confirm and Cancel) | true on confirm, false on cancel |
| `choose` | `title`, `items` (1–7 strings, each ≤ 63 bytes, required), `selected` (1-based row, may be omitted) | the selected row (1-based), or nil on cancel |

`toast(text)` shows a message on the screen for about 2 seconds without interrupting the app, and returns nothing. `text` is at most 95 bytes (47 bytes in 2.4 and earlier). If it does not fit on one line the host wraps it to at most three lines, and ends it with "..." if it still does not fit. On a host that implements 2.5, 2.1–2.4 packages may also use up to 95 bytes; for the text to display on older hosts as well, stay within 47 bytes or check `ctx.api.minor >= 5`.

They return nothing. Text that is too long returns `nil, "limit_exceeded"`. An empty `items`, or a `selected` outside the list, returns `nil, "invalid_argument"`. If a dialog, a text input, or (2.9) a docked input has not finished, the call returns `nil, "busy"`. In a lock-screen session, the call returns `nil, "inactive"`. When the session ends, an unfinished dialog is cancelled and the completion function is not called.

# 24. Front light (2.1)

Optional capability `frontlight`: `ctx.frontlight` exists when the device has a front light; otherwise it is nil. It is nil in a lock-screen session.

```lua
local f = ctx.frontlight:get()                       -- { on, brightness, warmth }
ctx.frontlight:set({ on = true, brightness = 20 })   -- write only the fields to change
ctx.frontlight:reset()                               -- back to the user's settings
```

`brightness` and `warmth` are integers 0–100 (for `warmth`, 0 is the coolest and 100 the warmest). `set` lasts only for this session and does not change system settings. `get` returns the values the app set. When the session ends (including entering the lock screen), the host calls `reset` automatically. If the system's night mode is running, `reset` hands the front light back to night mode. On a device without a warm light, `warmth` is always 0, and values written to it are ignored.

`set` and `reset` return nothing. An out-of-range value returns `nil, "invalid_argument"`.

# 25. Opening a system page (2.1)

```lua
if not online and ctx.system:can_open("settings.wifi") then
  ctx.system:open("settings.wifi")
end

-- 2.20: open a book in this app's folder with the reader
if ctx.system:can_open("file", { name = "dune.epub" }) then
  ctx.system:open("file", { name = "dune.epub" })
end

-- 2.27: the user tapped "Go to cloud sync"
if ctx.system:can_open("cloud.sync") then
  ctx.system:open("cloud.sync")
end
```

After the current callback returns, `open(target, opts)` ends this session (calling `on_leave`) and opens the target page. When the user comes back from that page, the app opens again as an entirely new session. To continue work after that, write it in `on_leave` to a file from section 9, or (2.2) keep it in `ctx.state` from section 28.

| Target | `opts` | Page |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `"settings.wifi"` | ignored | Wi-Fi settings |
| `"settings.bluetooth"` | ignored | Bluetooth settings |
| `"file"` (2.20) | `{ name = string }` | Opens the file named `name` in this app's folder (section 29) with the reader |
| `"book"` (2.20) | `{ id = string }` | Opens with the reader the book whose `id` is given by `ctx.reader:books()` or `current()` (section 22); from 2.33 it also accepts books from `library()` |
| `"cloud.sync"` (2.27) | ignored | Cloud sync page |
| `"settings.font"` (2.27) | ignored | The Ink App font page (section 7 "User-chosen font (2.17)") |
| `"settings.keyboard_dict"` (2.27) | ignored | Keyboard dictionary download page |
| `"app"` (2.32) | `{ id = string, open = table? }` | Opens another installed Ink App (needs the permission `apps`, section 34); when it ends, it returns to this app |

Later minor versions only add targets. `can_open(target, opts)` returns a boolean; it is false in every case where `open` would fail. When the target is not recognized or the session is a lock-screen session, `open` returns `nil, "invalid_argument"`. A successful `open` returns nothing. A Lua error is raised when `opts` is neither a table nor nil (section 0).

## Opening with the reader (2.20)

**Files.** `"file"` opens the file named `opts.name` in `/AppFiles/<app_id>/`. The name rules are the same as in section 29; only this one level is handled, and a path cannot be written. The reader is chosen by extension (case-insensitive): 2.20 can open `epub`, `txt`, `xtc`, `xtch` and `xtcz`, and more may be added later.

**Books.** `"book"` needs the permission `reader` and the optional capability `reader` (that is, `ctx.reader` is not nil); otherwise this target is not available to the app. `opts.id` accepts only books that `books()` and `current()` give right now; a book not in the recent list (for example one that appears only in `all_books()`) is treated as not recognized. (2.33) A package that declares `api` at least 2.33 may also use the `id` of any book that `library()` (section 22) gives, including a book that has never been opened; a book whose file has been deleted is treated as not recognized.

An opened book is the same as when the user opens it from the file manager: the reader saves progress per file, and the book is recorded in recent reading and reading statistics. A chapter, page or position cannot be specified. When the user comes back from the reader, they return to this app (a new session).

| Case | `open` returns | `can_open` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Success | nothing | true |
| Lock-screen session; `"book"` while `ctx.reader` is nil; `opts` lacks `name`/`id` or it is not a string; `name` is invalid | `nil, "invalid_argument"` | false |
| The file does not exist, or the same name is a sub-folder; no storage card; `id` is not recognized, or the book file has been deleted | `nil, "not_found"` | false |
| The extension has no reader (including `.xtapp` and a file with no extension) | `nil, "not_supported"` | false |

With only a target and no `opts`, `can_open("file")` is true in a normal session and `can_open("book")` is true when `ctx.reader` is not nil, meaning this host can open this kind of target for the app; use it to tell whether the host implements the 2.20 targets, without looking at `ctx.api.minor`. `open` without `opts` is treated as a missing field.

## Cloud sync, fonts and the keyboard dictionary (2.27)

**Cloud sync.** The page that `"cloud.sync"` opens is the same as opening cloud sync from the sidebar: when bound, it shows the sync list; when not bound, it shows the binding page. Binding verification, going online, pulling tasks, downloading and installing all follow that page's usual rules. When the user presses Back on the sync list or the binding page, they return to this app (a new session). When they open an already downloaded book or app in the sync list, that item opens by that page's usual rules, and they do not return to this app.

**Fonts.** `"settings.font"` opens the font page in the toolbox settings (section 7), where the user chooses the TTF the Ink App uses. When the user comes back from that page, they return to this app.

**Keyboard dictionary.** `"settings.keyboard_dict"` opens the system settings "General → Keyboard → Download dictionaries", where the user downloads the dictionaries that composition input (section 4) needs. When the user comes back from that page, they return to this app.

None of the three targets can specify content within the page, and `opts` is ignored. `can_open` is true in a normal session, and false in a lock-screen session or when the device has no such page; use it to tell whether the host implements the 2.27 targets, without looking at `ctx.api.minor`.

Call `open` only after an explicit user action (for example tapping "Go to cloud sync"). Do not open these pages automatically when a push succeeds, a download finishes, and so on: leaving the app on its own interrupts what the user is doing.

## Opening another Ink App (2.32)

```lua
-- manifest: "permissions": ["apps"]
if ctx.system:can_open("app", { id = "u-1a2b3c4d" }) then
  ctx.system:open("app", { id = "u-1a2b3c4d", open = { page = "today" } })
end
```

`"app"` needs the permission `apps` (section 34). `opts.id` is an `id` that `ctx.apps:list()` gives.

**Session.** The same as the other targets: after the current callback returns, this session ends (calling `on_leave`) and the target app opens.

**Returning to this app.** When the target app ends, this app opens again as a new session: when the target calls `ctx:quit()`, when Back is not handled (section 4), on a forced exit from a Back long press, or when it ends with an error, it returns to this app. Going to the home screen with a system key, entering the lock screen, or powering off follows the usual rules and does not return to this app. When the target app uses `"app"` to open a third app, the third app returns to the target app when it ends, not to this app: only one level of origin is remembered.

**`ctx.launch`.** The target app's `ctx.launch` for this session (section 33) is:

```lua
{ source = "app", from = "<this app's app_id>", open = { page = "today" } }
```

`open` is `opts.open` passed through unchanged; the host does not interpret it, and it is at most 191 bytes once encoded. When `opts.open` is not written, this field is absent. The target app can use `from` to show text like "Back to home".

| Case | `open` returns | `can_open` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Success | nothing | true |
| No `apps` permission; lock-screen session; `opts` lacks `id` or it is not a non-empty string; `id` is this app; `opts.open` is not a table, or it is over 191 bytes once encoded | `nil, "invalid_argument"` | false |
| `id` is not installed | `nil, "not_found"` | false |
| The target is `outdated` (an old interface version this host no longer runs, section 34), or its `requires` is not met by this device | `nil, "not_supported"` | false |

With only a target and no `opts`, `can_open("app")` is true in a normal session with the `apps` permission; use it to tell whether the host implements 2.32, without looking at `ctx.api.minor`. `open("app")` without `opts` is treated as a missing field.

## System actions (2.32)

```lua
-- the user tapped "Sleep" on the home screen
local ok, err = ctx.system:act("sleep")
```

`ctx.system:act(name)` makes the system do something the user could do with a physical key or a system menu. No permission is required.

| `name` | Action |
| --- | --- |
| `"sleep"` | Enters the lock screen, the same as a short press of the power key: ends this session (calling `on_leave`), the device sleeps and shows the lock screen; after waking, it is the same as when the user locks with the power key and then wakes it |
| `"power_off"` | Powers off. The host first shows the system confirmation dialog (during which `on_pause` and `on_resume`, section 23); when the user confirms, the session ends and the device powers off; when they cancel, it returns to this app and does nothing |
| `"refresh"` | The next frame after the current callback returns does a full refresh, the same as `ctx:invalidate("full")` |

**Only during user actions.** `"sleep"` and `"power_off"` may only be called in an `on_input` that delivers a key `up` or a pointer `up` (including functions it calls directly). Calling them in a timer, `on_load`, `on_tick`, a network completion, or any other callback returns `nil, "inactive"`: sleeping and powering off are decided by the user, and the app cannot make the device sleep or power off on its own. `"refresh"` is not subject to this rule.

| Case | Return |
| --- | --- |
| Success | nothing; after `sleep` or `power_off` is confirmed, the session then ends |
| `name` is not recognized | `nil, "invalid_argument"` |
| `sleep` or `power_off` called outside a user action; lock-screen session | `nil, "inactive"` |
| The `power_off` confirmation dialog is showing | `nil, "busy"` |
| `name` is not a string | Raises a Lua error (section 0) |

Use `ctx.frontlight` in section 24 for the front light and `ctx.screen:set_orientation` in section 3 for the orientation; they are not repeated here.

# 26. Encoding, hashes, and random bytes (2.1)

Required. Arguments and results are byte strings.

```lua
ctx.base64:encode(s, opts)   ctx.base64:decode(s)
ctx.hex:encode(s)            ctx.hex:decode(s)
ctx.url:encode(s)            ctx.url:decode(s)
ctx.url:query(t)             -- { q = "eink", page = 2 } -> "page=2&q=eink"

ctx.hash:sha256(s)  ctx.hash:sha1(s)  ctx.hash:md5(s)
ctx.hash:hmac_sha256(key, s)
ctx.hash:crc32(s)

ctx.random:bytes(n)
ctx.random:uuid()
```

- **base64**: uses the RFC 4648 standard alphabet, padded with `=`. When `opts.url` is true, the `-` `_` alphabet is used without padding. `decode` accepts both alphabets, and padding may be omitted.
- **hex**: `encode` outputs lowercase. `decode` accepts either case, and the length must be even.
- **url**: `encode` writes every byte outside `A–Z a–z 0–9 - . _ ~` as `%XX` (a space becomes `%20`). `decode` only decodes `%XX`; `+` is left unchanged. The keys of `query(t)` must be strings, and the values strings, numbers, or booleans. Items are joined in the byte order of the keys, and both keys and values are encoded with `encode`. An empty table yields `""`. At most 64 items are allowed.
- **hash**: returns the raw digest bytes (32 bytes for SHA-256, 20 for SHA-1, 16 for MD5), the same as Python `hashlib` `digest()`. For hexadecimal output, write `ctx.hex:encode(ctx.hash:sha256(s))`. `hmac_sha256` follows RFC 2104. `crc32` matches zlib `crc32`, but it is returned as a signed 32-bit integer (values above `0x7FFFFFFF` are negative).
- **random**: `bytes(n)` returns `n` hardware-random bytes, where `n` is an integer 1–1024. `uuid()` returns a version-4 UUID string (lowercase, with `-`). These are suitable for tokens and random seeds; `math.random` is not.

Input is limited to 1048576 bytes; longer input returns `nil, "limit_exceeded"`. An illegal character or an incorrect length during decoding returns `nil, "invalid_argument"`. Encryption and decryption are described in "Encryption (2.19)" below.

## Encryption (2.19)

Required, no permission needed. Arguments and results are byte strings.

```lua
local ct = ctx.crypto:aes_gcm_encrypt(key, iv, plaintext, aad)   -- ciphertext .. 16-byte tag
local pt, err = ctx.crypto:aes_gcm_decrypt(key, iv, ct, aad)     -- tag mismatch: nil, "auth_failed"

local priv, pub = ctx.crypto:x25519_keypair()        -- 32 bytes each
local pub2      = ctx.crypto:x25519_public(priv)
local shared    = ctx.crypto:x25519(priv, peer_pub)  -- 32 bytes

local priv, pub = ctx.crypto:p256_keypair()          -- 32 bytes; 65 bytes 0x04 || X || Y
local pub2      = ctx.crypto:p256_public(priv)
local shared    = ctx.crypto:p256_ecdh(priv, peer_pub) -- 32 bytes, the X coordinate of the shared point
```

- **AES-GCM**: `key` is 16, 24 or 32 bytes (AES-128 / 192 / 256), `iv` must be 12 bytes, and `aad` may be omitted, which is the same as `""`. `aes_gcm_encrypt` returns the ciphertext followed by a 16-byte authentication tag, the same as Python `cryptography` `AESGCM.encrypt`. The `ct` of `aes_gcm_decrypt` is at least 16 bytes; a tag mismatch (wrong key, `iv` or `aad`, or altered data) returns `nil, "auth_failed"` and gives no plaintext at all. An `iv` must never repeat under the same `key`, and the host does not check this: use `ctx.random:bytes(12)` for every message, or, as Noise does, 4 zero bytes plus an 8-byte counter.
- **X25519** (RFC 7748): `x25519_keypair()` generates the private key from the hardware random number generator, clamps it as RFC 7748 says, and returns the private key and the public key as two values; `x25519_public(priv)` computes the public key from the private key, for restoring from saved state; `x25519(priv, peer_pub)` returns the shared secret. Private and public keys are both 32 bytes. When the shared secret is all zeros (the peer gave a low-order point) it returns `nil, "invalid_argument"`.
- **P-256 ECDH**: the private key is a 32-byte big-endian scalar and the public key is the 65-byte uncompressed format (`0x04 || X || Y`). `p256_ecdh` returns the X coordinate of the shared point, the same as `ec.ECDH()` of `cryptography`. It returns `nil, "invalid_argument"` when `peer_pub` is not on the curve, or the private key is 0 or not less than the curve order.

They run synchronously and the time counts toward the current callback; one X25519 or P-256 operation is much slower than a hash, so call `ctx.budget:extend()` before doing several in a row. A wrong length returns `nil, "invalid_argument"`; an argument that is not a string raises a Lua error. `plaintext`, `ct` and `aad` are at most 1048576 bytes, and longer returns `nil, "limit_exceeded"`. The host does not keep keys: the private key is handed to the app, and the app stores it itself (section 9, section 28). Signatures, ChaCha20-Poly1305 and AES-CBC / CTR are not provided.

HKDF-SHA256 can be written with `ctx.hash:hmac_sha256`, so no separate call is provided:

```lua
local function hkdf_extract(salt, ikm)          -- an empty salt is equivalent to 32 zero bytes
  return ctx.hash:hmac_sha256(salt, ikm)
end

local function hkdf_expand(prk, info, len)      -- len ≤ 8160
  local out, t = {}, ""
  for i = 1, math.ceil(len / 32) do
    t = ctx.hash:hmac_sha256(prk, t .. info .. string.char(i))
    out[i] = t
  end
  return table.concat(out):sub(1, len)
end
```

# 27. Decompression, QR codes, and image decode (2.1)

```lua
local text = ctx.zlib:decompress(res.body)                     -- recognizes gzip or zlib
local code = ctx.qr:encode("https://example.com/r/42", { size = 240 })
local img  = ctx.image:decode(res.body, { max_w = 96, max_h = 96 })   -- optional capability image_decode
```

**Decompression** (required). `opts.format` is `"auto"` (the default), `"gzip"`, `"zlib"`, or `"raw"` (raw deflate). For gzip, the CRC-32 and the length at the end are checked. The result is at most 1048576 bytes; longer output returns `nil, "limit_exceeded"`. Damaged data or the wrong format returns `nil, "invalid_argument"`. Decompression needs about 70 KB of work space plus the size of the result; when the script heap cannot hold it, `not enough memory` is raised as in section 1, which `pcall` can catch. Compression is not provided.

**QR codes** (required). Returns a black-and-white runtime image (section 8) with a white margin of 4 modules on every side. `opts.size` is the desired side length in pixels (21–4096, default 200). The host uses the largest whole-number module size that does not exceed it; the actual side length is `code.width`. `opts.ecc` is `"low"`, `"medium"` (the default), `"quartile"`, or `"high"`. The content is at most 1024 bytes and contains no `\0`. If the content does not fit (too much content, or `size` smaller than the module count plus the white margin), the call returns `nil, "limit_exceeded"`.

**Image decode** (optional capability `image_decode`). Decodes PNG, JPEG, or BMP bytes into a runtime image, dithers it to the device's gray levels, and scales it proportionally to fit within `max_w × max_h` (1–4096, default the screen size). (2.18, a host fix that applies to packages of every version) When a PNG carries transparency (an alpha channel or `tRNS`), the decoded image has 1-bit transparency: after scaling, pixels less than 50% opaque are transparent and the rest are dithered by color without blending with the background, the same as PNG resources in the package (section 6, appendix A); `g:image`, layers, and `ctx.lockscreen:set_wallpaper` all honor it. A source image that is fully opaque carries no transparency; JPEG and BMP are always opaque. The transparency takes `ceil(w / 8)` bytes per row and counts toward the total runtime image bytes in section 8. (2.11) When `opts.gray` is true and `ctx.screen.gray_still` is 4, it decodes a 4-level image (colors 0, 5, 10, 15) for display in a gray frame; in a normal frame, the image is drawn as a dot pattern (section 3). When `gray_still` is 2, it still decodes to black and white. A `gray` value that is not a boolean returns `nil, "invalid_argument"`. The call runs synchronously, and its time counts against the current callback. A source image whose width or height exceeds 1024 returns `nil, "limit_exceeded"`. An unrecognized format returns `nil, "invalid_argument"`. Insufficient memory returns `nil, "out_of_memory"`. When used with section 14: a response body keeps at most 131072 bytes, so the server must reduce larger pictures first.

# 28. Automatic save (2.2)

```lua
ctx.state
ctx:save_state()
```

`ctx.state` is a table. The host saves it for the app and restores it when the next session starts. Use it for small, structured state such as game progress, settings, and scores; you do not need to write any save code. For data larger than the size limit below, binary data, or data you manage as several files, use the private files of section 9. For how to split continuously growing data, such as backpacks, logs, and the map, into files, see "When there is a lot of data" in section 9.

## When it is restored and saved

When a session starts, before the top level of the script and `on_load` run, the host loads the last saved content into `ctx.state`. If there is no save, or the save is damaged or cannot be read, it is an empty table. The main program and the lock-screen session (section 15) load the same save.

Each time a session ends, after `on_leave` returns (an error or a timeout in `on_leave` also counts as returning), the host reads `ctx.state` as it is at that moment and saves it. Every way of ending listed in the "how a session ends" table of section 2 triggers a save, including entering the lock screen and power-off. A session that ends because of an error before `on_leave` is not saved. A lock-screen session is not saved automatically.

If the content is the same as what was last restored or saved, the host writes nothing to the storage card.

The script can change the contents of the table or replace it entirely: `ctx.state = { level = 1 }`. The host saves the table that `ctx.state` points to at the moment of saving. If it is not a table at that moment, nothing is saved and the previous save is kept.

`ctx:save_state()` saves immediately and returns true. If `ctx.state` is not a table, it returns `nil, "invalid_argument"`. If the content is too large, it returns `nil, "limit_exceeded"`. If there is not enough memory to encode it, it returns `nil, "out_of_memory"`. If the storage card cannot be written, it returns `nil, "io_error"`. In the last three cases, the previous save is unchanged. The time spent writing the storage card counts against the current callback (see the reference values in section 9). Call it when progress in the middle of a session must not be lost (for example, when a round ends), so that a later error cannot discard it. Do not call it every frame.

## What can be saved

| Item | Rule |
| --- | --- |
| Values | Booleans, numbers, strings, and tables. An entry with any other value (functions, objects such as images) is not saved and is absent when read back |
| Keys | Strings and integers. An entry with any other key (float, boolean, table) is not saved |
| Arrays | A table whose keys are exactly 1 to `#t` is saved as an array. Other tables are saved by name, with integer keys written as decimal strings; when read back, such string keys become integer keys again. Do not use string keys that look like integers: `"12"` reads back as `12` |
| Numbers | An integer reads back as an integer. A float reads back as a float, but a float with no fractional part reads back as an integer (`2.0` reads back as `2`) |
| Strings | UTF-8 text with no zero bytes. To store arbitrary bytes, encode them with `ctx.base64` from section 26 first, or put them in a file from section 9 |
| Depth | At most 6 levels of tables under `ctx.state`. A deeper entry is not saved. A cycle is cut at this level |
| Size | At most 16384 bytes when encoded as JSON. If the content exceeds this, nothing is saved; it is not truncated |

## Where it is kept

Each app has one save, stored in the app's own directory. It is not one of the private files of section 9: it does not count against the section 9 quota and does not appear in `ctx.storage:list()`. It is kept across upgrades and deleted on uninstall (appendix B).

If power is lost during a save, the next restore gets either the old save or the new one.

The 0.8 `ctx.state` is stored in the same place and in the same format: when the same `app_id` is upgraded from 0.8 to 2.2, its progress appears unchanged in `ctx.state`.

## Versions

On a host that implements 2.2, `ctx.api.minor` is 2, and 2.0 and 2.1 packages also have `ctx.state` and are saved automatically (section 19). On a host at 2.1 or below, `ctx.state` and `save_state` are nil. An app that depends on the automatic save writes `"api": "2.2"` in its manifest. The automatic save is not an optional capability and requires no permission.

```lua
function on_load(ctx)
  local s = ctx.state
  s.v = s.v or 1                -- version of the save format, see appendix B
  s.best = s.best or 0
  s.board = s.board or new_board()
end

local function game_over(ctx, score)
  if score > ctx.state.best then ctx.state.best = score end
  ctx.state.board = new_board()
  ctx:save_state()              -- the result of a round must not be lost
end
```

## Idle games and offline progress

Idle and incremental games need to continue accumulating progress after they are closed. Once a session ends, the VM is destroyed and `on_tick` and timers are no longer called (section 2), so callbacks cannot add up the offline period. Instead, compute it from the wall clock on the next launch.

- Keep resources, levels, and the time of the last settlement in `ctx.state`. Local and global variables are lost when the session ends. Do not store values you can derive from levels, such as the output rate; compute them each time.
- Write defaults as `s.gold = s.gold or 0`. Writing `ctx.state = { gold = 0 }` in `on_load` replaces the save that was just loaded.
- Use a single settlement function: earnings = rate × (current `epoch_sec` − `epoch_sec` at the last settlement), then set the last settlement time to the current time. Call it on launch, on every `on_tick`, and before buying an upgrade. Online and offline progress take the same path, so pausing, locking, powering off, and different `on_tick` intervals on different devices (section 2) do not change the result.
- If the current time is earlier than the last settlement (the clock was set back), do not settle and do not move the last settlement time back; otherwise, that period is credited again once the clock is corrected. Set a cap on the offline duration: it is part of the game design and also prevents gains from setting the clock forward.
- When `valid` is false, `epoch_sec` is nil (section 12): do not settle and do not change the last settlement time. For the online part, you can instead add up intervals of `ctx.clock:millis()`, which is valid only within the current boot.
- Compute offline earnings with a formula in one step; do not simulate second by second: `on_load` is limited to 2000 ms (section 2). If you do need stepwise simulation, use coarse steps or call `ctx.budget:extend()`.
- Integers are 32-bit and wrap to negative past `2147483647` (section 1). Use floats for resources that may exceed that value: about 7 significant digits, with a maximum of about `3.4e38`. A number without a fractional part loads back as an integer. After loading, write `s.gold = s.gold + 0.0` to convert it back to a float; otherwise, later multiplication is done on integers and may wrap.
- Call `ctx:save_state()` after buying upgrades, prestige, and similar actions. Nothing is saved automatically when a session ends with an error or power is lost suddenly. With wall-clock settlement, only the actions since the last save are lost, and the output during that time is credited as offline progress on the next launch.
- To show resources on the lock screen (section 15), compute them in the lock-screen script with the same formula, and do not write them back to `ctx.state`.

```lua
local OFFLINE_CAP = 8 * 3600            -- credit at most 8 hours offline
local offline_gain = 0                  -- offline earnings credited on this launch, for display only

local function rate(s)                  -- output per second: derived from levels, not stored
  return s.miners * 1.5
end

local function settle(ctx)
  local s = ctx.state
  local now = ctx.clock:now().epoch_sec
  if not now then return 0 end          -- clock not valid: don't settle, don't touch last_sec
  local last = s.last_sec or now
  if now < last then return 0 end       -- clock set back: same, never move last_sec back
  local dt = now - last
  if dt > OFFLINE_CAP then dt = OFFLINE_CAP end
  local gain = rate(s) * dt
  s.gold = s.gold + gain
  s.last_sec = now
  return gain
end

function on_load(ctx)
  local s = ctx.state
  s.gold = (s.gold or 0) + 0.0          -- may load back as an integer: turn it back into a float
  s.miners = s.miners or 1
  offline_gain = settle(ctx)
  ctx:set_tick(1000)
end

function on_tick(ctx, dt_ms)
  settle(ctx)
  ctx:invalidate()
end

local function buy_miner(ctx)
  local s = ctx.state
  settle(ctx)                           -- settle up to now at the old rate first
  local cost = 10 * 1.15 ^ s.miners
  if s.gold < cost then return false end
  s.gold = s.gold - cost
  s.miners = s.miners + 1
  ctx:save_state()
  return true
end
```

# 29. App files (2.9)

A folder on the storage card that the user can see. The user puts books, word lists, images, and settings in it for the app to read, and the app writes exported notes and generated files to it for the user to take. Hosts must implement it. No permission is required.

```lua
local list, err = ctx.files:list()        -- { { name = "Three-Body.txt", size = 1834567 }, ... }
local head = ctx.files:read("Three-Body.txt", 0, 4096)
ctx.files:write("Excerpts.md", text)      -- replaces the whole file
ctx.files:append("Log.txt", line .. "\n")
ctx:log("Put files in this folder on the storage card: " .. ctx.files.path)
```

**Folder.** Each app has one: `AppFiles/<app_id>/` under the root of the storage card. `ctx.files.path` is `"/AppFiles/<app_id>"`; use it to tell the user where to put files. The first time in a session that any `ctx.files` function is called, the host creates the folder if it does not exist; an app that never calls these functions has no folder. The main program and the lock screen share it. Other apps cannot see it. **Neither uninstall nor upgrade deletes it**: it holds the user's files. The user can add files by connecting to a computer or by phone transfer, and can also change them while the app runs; each call sees the storage card as it is at the moment of the call.

Division of work with the private files in section 9: the app's own data (caches, indexes, progress) goes in section 9; the user cannot see it, and uninstall deletes it. Files the user should see, add, or take go here.

**Names.** Only files directly in the folder count; subfolders are not entered. A name is 1–128 bytes of UTF-8. It contains no control characters (U+0000–U+001F and U+007F) and none of `/ \ : * ? " < > | ~`, does not start with `.`, does not end with `.` or a space, and the part before `.` is not `CON` `PRN` `AUX` `NUL` `COM1`–`COM9` `LPT1`–`LPT9` (case-insensitive). An illegal name returns `nil, "invalid_argument"` (`exists` returns false). The storage card is case-insensitive: `A.txt` and `a.txt` are the same file, and `list()` returns the spelling stored on the card. Names are compared byte by byte, with no Unicode normalization.

| Call | File exists | File is absent |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `read(name, offset, len)` | at most `len` bytes from `offset`; `""` when `offset` is at or past the end | `nil, "not_found"` |
| `write(name, data)` | replaces the whole file, returns true | creates it, returns true |
| `append(name, data)` | appends to the end, returns true | creates it, returns true |
| `remove(name)` | deletes it, returns true | returns true |
| `exists(name)` | true | false (also false for an illegal name or no storage card) |
| `size(name)` | the byte count | `nil, "not_found"` |

**Reading.** `offset` is optional, defaults to 0, and must not be negative. `len` is optional, defaults to 65536, and ranges from 1 to 65536; a value above 65536 returns `nil, "limit_exceeded"`, and other illegal values return `nil, "invalid_argument"`. A returned string shorter than `len` means the end of the file was reached. Read a large file in chunks, a few chunks per callback, and continue with `ctx:after`:

```lua
local function read_on(ctx, name, pos)
  for _ = 1, 4 do
    local chunk, err = ctx.files:read(name, pos, 65536)
    if not chunk then return show_error(err) end
    if chunk == "" then return done() end
    pos = pos + #chunk
    take(chunk)
  end
  ctx:after(1, function(ctx) read_on(ctx, name, pos) end)
end
```

A chunk may end in the middle of a UTF-8 character. To draw it (section 7 accepts only valid UTF-8), use `utf8.len` to find the last complete character and carry the remaining bytes over to the start of the next chunk. To paginate text, use `font:layout` from section 7.

**Writing.** `data` is a string and can contain any bytes. `write` and `append` accept at most 262144 bytes per call; more returns `nil, "limit_exceeded"`, and the file is unchanged. If power fails during `write`, a later read sees either the whole old content or the whole new content. If power fails during `append`, the original content is unchanged, and the appended part may be partly written or not written at all. If an append would make the file larger than 2147483647 bytes, it returns `nil, "limit_exceeded"`.

**Quota.** The folder holds at most 512 files (only files with legal names count). When it already holds 512, a `write` or `append` that creates a new file returns `nil, "limit_exceeded"`; changing an existing file is not affected. There is no limit on total bytes; when the storage card is full, the call returns `nil, "io_error"`. If the user has added more than 512 files, `list()` returns `nil, "limit_exceeded"`, and calls by name work as usual.

**Listing.** `list()` returns an array of `{ name, size }` items, sorted by the byte order of the names. Subfolders and files with illegal names (such as `.DS_Store`) are not listed. If a subfolder has the same name as a file, `read` and `size` treat the file as absent, and `remove` returns `nil, "io_error"`. If the folder does not exist or holds no files, it returns an empty table.

A failed read or write, or a missing storage card, returns `nil, "io_error"`. Insufficient memory returns `nil, "out_of_memory"`. The time spent reading and writing the storage card counts against the current callback's limit (see the reference values in section 9). Read a large file across several `ctx:after` callbacks; do not read or write every frame in `on_tick` or `on_draw`.

**Opening with the reader (2.20).** The reader can open an `epub`, `txt`, `xtc`, `xtch` or `xtcz` file in the app folder through `ctx.system:open("file", { name = name })` (section 25); when reading finishes, it returns to this app.

## Public folders (2.31)

Several folders shared by all apps on the storage card. Books, images, fonts, and documents the user puts in can be read and written by any app that declares the permission; files an app writes are also available to other apps and the user. The `folders` permission is required (only packages with `api` at least 2.31 may declare it); without the declaration, `ctx.files.folder` is nil. Hosts must implement them.

```lua
local pub = ctx.files:folder("Public")
pub:mkdir("wordlists/CET-4")
pub:write("wordlists/CET-4/list.txt", text)
for _, e in ipairs(pub:list("wordlists")) do ctx:log(e.name .. (e.dir and "/" or "")) end
local books = ctx.files:folder("Pushed Books")
local head = books:read("Three-Body.epub", 0, 4096)
```

**Folders.** `ctx.files:folder(name)` returns a folder object. `name` must be one of the following (case-sensitive); any other name returns `nil, "invalid_argument"`. Each folder is under the root of the storage card, and `folder.path` is `"/" .. name`, used to tell the user where it is.

| `name` | Purpose | Subfolders |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Public` | exchanging files between apps, and between apps and the user | allowed |
| `Documents` | documents | allowed |
| `Downloads` | downloaded files | allowed |
| `Pictures` | pictures | allowed |
| `Music` | audio | allowed |
| `Pushed Books` | books pushed by cloud sync; the reader reads from here | single level |
| `Pushed Images` | images pushed by cloud sync; lock-screen images are chosen from here | single level |
| `Pushed Fonts` | fonts pushed by cloud sync; the reader chooses from here | single level |
| `Fonts` | fonts the user adds; the reader chooses from here | single level |

When a folder does not exist, `folder()` still returns the object: `list` gets an empty table, and the host creates it on the first `write`, `append`, or `mkdir`. Uninstall and upgrade do not delete the files in it. The system itself also reads and writes these folders (cloud-sync pushes, the reader, the lock screen); each call sees the storage card as it is at the moment of the call.

**Paths.** Folder-object calls take a path rather than a name. A path is made of segments separated by `/`; each segment follows the name rules above (1–128 bytes, forbidden characters, must not start with `.`, and so on), at most 8 segments, 255 bytes in total, must not start or end with `/`, and has no empty segment. Folders marked "single level" accept only one segment. An illegal path returns `nil, "invalid_argument"` (`exists` returns false). The case rules are the same as above.

| Call | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `list(dir)` | When `dir` is omitted, lists the folder itself; otherwise lists that subfolder. Returns an array of `{ name, size, dir }` items: `dir` is true for a subfolder, and its `size` is 0. Sorted by the byte order of the names; items with illegal names are not listed. If the subfolder does not exist, `nil, "not_found"`; over 512 items, `nil, "limit_exceeded"`. Single-level folders do not list subfolders; passing `dir` returns `nil, "invalid_argument"` |
| `exists(path)` | whether the file is there; a subfolder counts as not there |
| `size(path)` | the byte count; if absent, `nil, "not_found"` |
| `read(path, offset, len)` | same as `ctx.files:read` |
| `write(path, data)` | same as `ctx.files:write` (replaces the whole file; on power failure, either the whole old content or the whole new content); missing parent subfolders are created automatically |
| `append(path, data)` | same as `ctx.files:append`; missing parent subfolders are created automatically |
| `remove(path)` | deletes the file; returns true even when absent; if it is a subfolder, `nil, "io_error"` |
| `mkdir(path)` | creates a subfolder, creating missing parents too; returns true if it already exists; if a file with the same name exists, `nil, "io_error"`. On a single-level folder, `nil, "invalid_argument"` |
| `rmdir(path)` | deletes an empty subfolder; returns true even when absent; if it has contents or is a file, `nil, "io_error"`. On a single-level folder, `nil, "invalid_argument"` |

Public folders have no 512-file quota and no limit on total bytes; the per-call limits, error codes, and time counting against the callback limit are the same as for the app folder above. A temporary file left by a half-finished `write` does not appear in `list`; the host cleans it up the next time that path is accessed.

**Division of work with the app folder.** Files meant only for this app and the user go in `ctx.files`'s own folder; use the public folders only for files meant for other apps, or to read books and images pushed by the system. Deleting or overwriting a file in a public folder affects the user and other apps; ask the user in a dialog first (section 23).

local head = ctx.files:read("Three-Body.txt", 0, 4096)
ctx.files:write("Excerpts.md", text)      -- replaces the whole file
ctx.files:append("Log.txt", line .. "\n")
ctx:log("Put files in this folder on the storage card: " .. ctx.files.path)

# 30. Native inference (2.18)

`ctx.nn` runs bounded model data that the app passes in. It contains no app rules or built-in models, and it does not read paths, download files, or run native code. A host that implements 2.18 must provide it in a normal session, and no permission is required; `ctx.capabilities.nn` is true in a normal session and false in a lock-screen session, where `ctx.nn` is nil. This field is for compatibility with older firmware and for telling sessions apart; a host must not turn off the interface in a normal session just because it lacks a dedicated inference SDK. On an older host that does not have this field, treat it as unavailable.

A package that must use inference writes `"api": "2.18"` and may also list `nn` in `requires`. A package that can degrade keeps an older version and checks `ctx.capabilities.nn == true`. `requires` is checked in the normal session; a package is not refused just because it also carries a lock-screen script.

```lua
local model, err = ctx.nn:load(model_bytes)
if not model then return end
local info = model:info()
local nn_job, err = model:run(input_bytes, { timeout_ms = 30000 }, function(ctx, result, err)
  if result then
    -- an F32 little-endian byte string joined in info.outputs order.
    ctx:invalidate()
  end
end)
-- when the result is no longer needed:
if nn_job then nn_job:cancel() end
model:close()
```

## Models and quota

`ctx.nn:formats()` returns a new array of strings. In 2.18 it is `{ "fwnn-1", "fwnn-2", "fwnn-3" }`, in a fixed order. The query loads no model, allocates no arena, and uses no model or job slot; it can be called while a model is loaded or while inference is running. Changing the returned array does not affect the host, and later queries still return the complete array. Unreleased 2.18 experimental firmware may lack this method, or may support only one of the earlier formats; the app must check that the method exists and that the array contains the format its actual model needs, for example `fwnn-3`, and must not infer it from the `nn` capability or the API version alone. A host that implements 2.18 for real must support all three formats and must not add a separate optional `nn_int8` capability.

`ctx.nn:load(bytes)` accepts a complete FWNN v1, v2, or v3 model byte string and returns a model handle or `nil, err`. [FWNN v1](../../contracts/v2/formats/fwnn-1.md) supports Conv2D, Dense, ReLU, Add, GlobalMeanMax, Tanh, and ReshapeCopy; [FWNN v2](../../contracts/v2/formats/fwnn-2.md) keeps these F32 operators and adds symmetric INT8 Conv/Dense, quantization/dequantization, mixed-precision Add, INT8 pooling to F32, and INT8 Dense to F32. In v2 the internal weights and activations may be INT8, and multiply-accumulate uses INT32; [FWNN v3](../../contracts/v2/formats/fwnn-3.md) further adds W8A32 Conv/Dense, decoding I8 weights with a per-output-channel F32 scale and computing along the F32 path, without quantizing activations. The inputs an app passes in and all the outputs it receives are still little-endian IEEE-754 binary32. Tensors use an HWC contiguous layout, with batch 1. The byte string may contain NUL.

At most one model is open per session; a second `load` returns `nil, "busy"`, and after a `close` another model can be loaded. The host holds the model data until the model is closed, so the app can drop its original variable. A corrupt, truncated, or unknown magic/version/operator, an illegal reference or shape, or a non-finite constant returns `nil, "invalid_argument"`; an unsupported format is not reported as `not_supported`.

Limits: 2097152 bytes for the model, 1048576 bytes for the arena, at most 256 tensors, 256 operators, and 16 outputs, at most 16384 bytes of outputs in total, and an estimated graph workload of 100000000; for the remaining dimensions and the per-step limits, see the format documents. Exceeding a limit returns `nil, "limit_exceeded"`. These limits are not memory reservations or performance guarantees. The model, input, arena, objects, and results count against the existing Lua heap; a `load` that fails to allocate the model or arena returns `nil, "out_of_memory"`, and other exhausted Lua allocations are handled as in section 1.

`model:info()` returns a new information table: `format` is `"fwnn-1"`, `"fwnn-2"`, or `"fwnn-3"`; `input={height,width,channels,bytes}`; `outputs={{height,width,channels,bytes,offset},...}`; plus `model_bytes`, `arena_bytes`, `output_bytes`, and `work`. `outputs` is in model output order, and `offset` starts at 0 and is in bytes; the `bytes` of `input`/`outputs` all mean external F32 byte counts, and `output_bytes` is the byte count of all outputs. `arena_bytes` already includes the v2/v3 computation scratch, and a backend must not implicitly allocate a workspace beyond this budget. `work` is an estimated scalar workload, not milliseconds or a pure multiply-accumulate count; v3 also counts the per-output-channel weight decoding work. Changing the returned table does not affect the model.

## Reusable workspace

An app that needs to load several models one after another, or to run inference many times, can reserve a workspace first, reducing the large-allocation failures caused by heap fragmentation. It is capacity that the app holds explicitly, not a hidden cache of the host, and it does not change the FWNN format or the external F32LE inputs and outputs.

```lua
local workspace, err = ctx.nn:workspace({ model_bytes = 65536, arena_bytes = 32768 })
if not workspace then return end
local model, err = workspace:load({ first_chunk, second_chunk })
-- model:info/run/close are the same as for the object a normal load returns.
if model then model:close() end
workspace:close()
```

`ctx.nn:workspace(opts)` returns a workspace or `nil, err`. `opts` is required; `model_bytes` and `arena_bytes` are both required positive integers, at most 2097152 and 1048576 bytes respectively, and at most 3145728 bytes per workspace in total. Non-positive, non-integer, NaN, or Inf returns `invalid_argument`; exceeding the hard limit returns `limit_exceeded`; a parameter or field of the wrong type raises a Lua error by the general rule, and unknown `opts` fields are ignored. The capacity does not need to be filled in multiples of an alignment. On creation, the two buffers and the objects are reserved at once and all count against the existing Lua heap; a failure to reserve them explicitly or to establish their ownership returns `nil, "out_of_memory"` and leaves no partial workspace. The limits do not guarantee that the allocation succeeds.

A session can hold several workspaces, each subject to the limits above and to the shared Lua heap budget. Creating a workspace loads no model and uses no model or job slot, so it is allowed even while a model is open or a job is running. There is still only one open model and one computing or awaiting-delivery job in the session; a normal `ctx.nn:load` and every `workspace:load` share this limit. The mere existence of a workspace does not make a normal `load` return `busy`; the memory it uses may make later allocations return `out_of_memory`.

`workspace:load(chunks)` accepts a contiguous array of 1–128 items, each a binary string that may contain NUL; an empty byte-string item is also allowed. A non-table or a non-string element raises a type error; an empty array, a hole, more than 128 items, and a non-positive, non-integer, or out-of-range numeric key returns `nil, "invalid_argument"`. Non-numeric keys are ignored, and a metatable must not be used to fill in missing array items. All chunks are copied into the reserved model buffer in order, without the caller joining them first; after a successful return, the `chunks` table or the chunk strings are no longer relied on, and changing the table or dropping the variables does not affect the model.

Before loading, the session's single model slot is checked; if a model is already open or a job is running, it returns `busy`, and it must not overwrite the data of another workspace or of a normal model. If the total bytes of the chunks exceed the reserved `model_bytes`, or if a valid graph requires more `arena_bytes` than the reserved `arena_bytes`, it returns `limit_exceeded`. The model is still checked by the same complete FWNN validator; a corrupt or unknown format and the like still return `invalid_argument`, and the existing hard limits on the graph still apply. An insufficient workspace is not enlarged automatically and does not borrow space from elsewhere. Each `load` may allocate a small amount of model-handle or ownership metadata; an explicit failure to allocate it returns `out_of_memory`, but it must not allocate a whole model or arena block again. A failure leaves no open model and no residual `busy`; the workspace stays open and can be retried on the next `load`, and the buffer contents after a failure are not guaranteed.

For a workspace model, `info().model_bytes` and `info().arena_bytes` are what this graph actually needs, not the reserved capacity. A workspace model's `model:close()` cancels its job and releases the single model slot; the workspace keeps holding the two reserved buffers, and the next `load` can load a graph of a different format or size. It does not change the existing semantics of a normal `ctx.nn:load` model, which releases its dedicated buffer reference after close.

`workspace:close()` returns true and is idempotent; it closes its currently open model, cancels that model's undelivered jobs without calling back, and then releases the reserved buffer references. Closing another idle workspace must not affect the current model or job. Afterwards, `load` on that workspace returns `nil, "invalid_handle"`, and `info`/`run` on its closed model also return `invalid_handle`; closing the model or workspace again still succeeds. Closing releases ownership, and the actual bytes are reclaimed by the Lua GC, with no promise to return physical memory immediately.

An open model must safely hold its owning workspace; after the caller drops the workspace variable and the GC runs, the model can still run. A workspace that holds no model and is no longer referenced by the caller can be reclaimed by the GC, so no explicit `close` is needed to prevent a leak. The semantics are the same for coroutines in the same VM. When the session ends, all workspaces, models, and jobs are released; once the end flow begins, creating or loading into a workspace is not accepted and returns `inactive`, and `load` on an already-closed object is still handled as `invalid_handle`.

## Running and callbacks

`model:run(input_bytes, opts, fn)` returns a job handle or `nil, err`. `opts` may be nil, or it may be omitted as `model:run(input_bytes, fn)`; `fn` is always required. The input length must exactly equal `info.input.bytes`, and every F32 value must be finite, otherwise it returns `nil, "invalid_argument"`. Once the method accepts, the input has already been copied, so the caller need not keep the original variable. At most one job may be computing or awaiting delivery of its result per session; a further `run` returns `nil, "busy"`.

`opts.timeout_ms` is an integer from 1 to 30000, default 30000. A float that is exactly an integer is also accepted; a non-integer, NaN, Inf, or an out-of-range value returns `nil, "invalid_argument"`. A parameter of the wrong type raises a Lua error as in section 0, and unknown `opts` fields are ignored. The deadline is counted from when `run` is accepted, on the monotonic wall clock, and includes paused time; when it expires, `fn(ctx, nil, "limit_exceeded")` is called.

`run` does not run the completion function inside the current call stack. On success, `fn(ctx, result, nil)` is called once; `result` is the F32LE byte string concatenated in `info.outputs` order. When the computation produces NaN/Inf, `fn(ctx, nil, "invalid_argument")` is called; no half-finished result is delivered. The active job slot is cleared before delivery, so the completion function can `run` again. The completion function runs in the Lua task it belongs to and is subject to the 1000 ms callback budget of section 2.

The host advances the computation in bounded small slices, processing pending events between slices. During a pause it neither advances nor delivers; after resuming it first redraws as in section 2, then checks the job deadline first, and only then advances or delivers. The format validation, input validation/copying, and result packaging of `load` still have synchronous cost. Slicing is not a hard real-time latency promise, and it does not require threads or multiple cores.

## Cancel, close, and session

`nn_job:cancel()` returns nothing; it has no effect on a job that has already finished or been cancelled. After cancelling, the completion function is no longer called, and a result that was computed but not delivered is discarded. Once the method returns, the active job slot can be reused; an old job handle cannot cancel a job created later. The semantics are the same as cancelling a network request in section 14.

`model:close()` returns true and is idempotent; it cancels this model's job and suppresses callbacks that have not yet been delivered. After close, `info`/`run` return `nil, "invalid_handle"`. A normal `load` allocates a dedicated arena at load time and reuses it across several `run` calls; a workspace model borrows the reserved arena. `cancel` and completion release the job/callback references but keep the open model's arena. Closing a normal model releases the model data and arena it holds; closing a workspace model makes the reserved buffer available for that workspace to load into again. The actual Lua memory is reclaimed by the GC, with no promise to return physical bytes immediately.

Coroutines in the same VM can call these methods; cancel and close have the same effect as on the main Lua thread. When the session ends, is force-exited, or errors, the model is cancelled and closed automatically, and inference stops before `on_leave` begins; once the session end flow is entered, new work is not accepted, `load` returns `nil, "inactive"`, and `info`/`run` on a closed model are still handled as `nil, "invalid_handle"`. The next session does not receive an old result.

FWNN v2 specifies the numeric semantics of the internal INT8/INT32; it promises no SIMD, ESP-DL, ESP-NN, dual core, or specific speedup. Fixed-point rescaling is compared exactly by the double-round defined in the format; floating-point results on different platforms are compared by a tolerance validated for the model, and all outputs must not be assumed to be byte-identical. Format conversion and quantization calibration cannot be guaranteed to preserve the original model's quality; the model author must verify the numeric error, the task quality, and the memory separately. Host timing cannot substitute for measuring on the real device.

FWNN v3's W8A32 only compresses the weight storage; activations and accumulation stay F32. Each weight is first decoded with its scale and then used in the dot product; the scale must not be moved after the sum to change the rounding path. It does not use v2's activation calibration or Q31 rescaling, and it does not promise to be faster. You must still verify numeric consistency with the original decoded F32 model, the real memory, and the timing on the real device.

local model, err = ctx.nn:load(model_bytes)
if not model then return end
local info = model:info()
local nn_job, err = model:run(input_bytes, { timeout_ms = 30000 }, function(ctx, result, err)
  if result then
    -- an F32 little-endian byte string joined in info.outputs order.
    ctx:invalidate()
  end
end)
-- when the result is no longer needed:
if nn_job then nn_job:cancel() end
model:close()
